Suppose we're given that [MATH: X>s,] and we want to determine the probability that [MATH: X>s+t.] In other words, we wish to compute the conditional probability
[MATH: P(X>s+t \,\big|\, X>s).]

Content:
By the definition of conditional probability, we have that
[MATH: P(X>s+t \, \big|\, X>s) = \dfrac{P\big((X> s+t) \cap (X > s)\big)}{P(X>s)}.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: X>s+t] implies that [MATH: X>s,] therefore
[MATH: P\big((X> s+t) \cap (X > s)\big) = P(X > s+t).]

Content:
So, the above conditional probability simplifies to
[MATH: P(X>s+t \,\big|\, X>s) = \dfrac{P(X> s+t )}{P(X>s)}.]

Content:
Next, let's recall how to calculate [MATH: P(X > a)] for some [MATH: a>0{:}]
[MATH: P(X > a)|= 1 − P(X < a); = 1 − ∫_{0}^{a}λe^{− λx}dx; = 1 + e^{− λx}|_{0}^{a}; = 1 + e^{− λa} − e^{0}; = e^{− λa}.]

Content:
Therefore, we can use this fact to calculate [MATH: P(X> s+t )] and [MATH: P(X>s)]

Content:
[MATH: P(X > s + t|X > s)|= (P(X > s + t))/(P(X > s)); = (e^{− λ(s + t)})/(e^{− λs}); = (e^{− λs} ⋅ e^{− λt})/(e^{− λs}); = (e^{− λs} ⋅ e^{− λt})/(e^{− λs}); = e^{− λt}]

Content:
Finally, notice that [MATH: e^{-\lambda t} = P(X > t).] So, we have proved the following property:
[MATH: P(X>s+t \big| X>s) = P(X > t).]

Content:
This property is called memoryless property. It can be proved that the exponential distribution is the only continuous distribution with this property (note that the geometric distribution is the only discrete distribution with the memoryless property).

Content:
Intuitively, the memoryless property states that the probability of an event occurring after a certain amount of time has already elapsed is independent of how much time has passed. This means that the distribution "forgets" what has happened before time [MATH: s.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A continuous random variable [MATH: X] follows an exponential distribution if it has the following probability density function:

Content:
[MATH: {λe^{− λx},|x ≥ 0; 0,|otherwise]

Content:
The rate parameter [MATH: \lambda] is a positive real number, and [MATH: e\approx 2.71828] is Euler's number.

Content:
If a random variable [MATH: X] follows an exponential distribution, we write

Content:
[MATH: X\sim \textrm{Exp}(\lambda).]

Content:
The exponential distribution models the amount of continuous space or time between two events. In a future lesson, we will learn how to model situations using the exponential distribution. But for now, let's get some practice working with the PDF to compute probabilities.

---

Item 2 — Example: Computing a "Less Than" Probability With the Exponential Distribution

Example Prompt:
Given that the random variable [MATH: X\sim \textrm{Exp}\left(1\right),] calculate [MATH: P\left(X < 2\right).] Round your final answer to four decimal places.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
An exponential random variable [MATH: X] with rate [MATH: \lambda] has the following probability density function:

[MATH: {λe^{− λx},|x ≥ 0; 0,|otherwise]

We're given that

[MATH: X\sim \textrm{Exp} \left( 1 \right).]

So, [MATH: X] has the following probability density function:

[MATH: {e^{− x},|x ≥ 0; 0,|otherwise]

Therefore, we can calculate [MATH: P\left(X < 2\right)] as follows:

[MATH: P(X < 2)|= ∫_{0}^{2}f(x)dx; = ∫_{0}^{2}e^{− x}dx; = − e^{− x}|_{0}^{2}; = − e^{− 2} + e^{0}; ≈ 0.8647]

---

Item 5 — Example: Computing a "Greater Than" Probability With the Exponential Distribution

Explanation:
An exponential random variable [MATH: X] with rate [MATH: \lambda] has the following probability density function:

[MATH: {λe^{− λx},|x ≥ 0; 0,|otherwise]

We're given that

[MATH: X\sim \textrm{Exp} \left( \dfrac 23 \right).]

So, [MATH: X] has the following probability density function:

[MATH: {(2)/(3)e^{− 2x/3},|x ≥ 0; 0,|otherwise]Therefore, we can calculate [MATH: P\left(X \geq 3\right)] as follows:

[MATH: P(X ≥ 3)|= ∫_{3}^{∞}f(x)dx; = ∫_{3}^{∞}(2)/(3)e^{− 2x/3}dx; = − e^{− 2x/3}|_{3}^{∞}; = e^{− 2}; ≈ 0.1353]

We're given that

So, [MATH: X] has the following probability density function:

[MATH: {2e^{− 2x},|x ≥ 0; 0,|otherwise]Therefore, we can calculate [MATH: P\left(\dfrac 12 < X < 2\right)] as follows:

Item 11 — Tutorial: The Memoryless Property

Content:
Consider a random variable [MATH: X \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda),] and two positive real numbers [MATH: s, t.]

Content:
Suppose we're given that [MATH: X>s,] and we want to determine the probability that [MATH: X>s+t.] In other words, we wish to compute the conditional probability
[MATH: P(X>s+t \,\big|\, X>s).]

Content:
By the definition of conditional probability, we have that
[MATH: P(X>s+t \, \big|\, X>s) = \dfrac{P\big((X> s+t) \cap (X > s)\big)}{P(X>s)}.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: X>s+t] implies that [MATH: X>s,] therefore
[MATH: P\big((X> s+t) \cap (X > s)\big) = P(X > s+t).]

Content:
So, the above conditional probability simplifies to
[MATH: P(X>s+t \,\big|\, X>s) = \dfrac{P(X> s+t )}{P(X>s)}.]

Content:
Next, let's recall how to calculate [MATH: P(X > a)] for some [MATH: a>0{:}]
[MATH: P(X > a)|= 1 − P(X < a); = 1 − ∫_{0}^{a}λe^{− λx}dx; = 1 + e^{− λx}|_{0}^{a}; = 1 + e^{− λa} − e^{0}; = e^{− λa}.]

Content:
Therefore, we can use this fact to calculate [MATH: P(X> s+t )] and [MATH: P(X>s)]

Content:
[MATH: P(X > s + t|X > s)|= (P(X > s + t))/(P(X > s)); = (e^{− λ(s + t)})/(e^{− λs}); = (e^{− λs} ⋅ e^{− λt})/(e^{− λs}); = (e^{− λs} ⋅ e^{− λt})/(e^{− λs}); = e^{− λt}]

Content:
Finally, notice that [MATH: e^{-\lambda t} = P(X > t).] So, we have proved the following property:
[MATH: P(X>s+t \big| X>s) = P(X > t).]

Content:
This property is called memoryless property. It can be proved that the exponential distribution is the only continuous distribution with this property (note that the geometric distribution is the only discrete distribution with the memoryless property).

Content:
Intuitively, the memoryless property states that the probability of an event occurring after a certain amount of time has already elapsed is independent of how much time has passed. This means that the distribution "forgets" what has happened before time [MATH: s.]

Content:
We'll discuss how the memoryless property is used for mathematical modeling in future lessons.

---

Item 12 — Tutorial: A Worked Example

Content:
Given that the random variable [MATH: X\sim \textrm{Exp}(2),] let's calculate the following probability:
[MATH: P\left(X > \dfrac32 \,\bigg|\, X > \dfrac12\right)]

Content:
Given a random variable [MATH: X \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)] and two positive real numbers [MATH: s, t,] the memoryless property of the exponential distribution states that
[MATH: P(X>s+t \, \big|\, X>s) = P(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}.]

Content:
In our case, we have
[MATH: \lambda = 2, \qquad s=\dfrac 12,\qquad s+t=\dfrac32.]

Content:
From this, we can find [MATH: t] as follows:
[MATH: t = (t+s) - s = \dfrac32-\dfrac12 = 1]

Content:
Substituting these values into the above formula, we get
[MATH: P(X > (3)/(2)|X > (1)/(2))|= e^{− λt}; = e^{− (2) ⋅ (1)}; = e^{− 2}; = (1)/(e^{2}); ≈ 0.135]

---

Explanation:
Given a random variable [MATH: X \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)] and two positive real numbers [MATH: s, t,] the memoryless property of the exponential distribution states that
[MATH: P(X>s+t \, \big |\, X>s) = P(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}.]

We can compute the complementary conditional probability as follows:
[MATH: P(X\leq s+t \, \big|\, X>s) = 1-P(X>s+t \, \big |\, X>s) = 1-e^{-\lambda t}]

In our case, we have [MATH: \lambda = 4,] [MATH: s=5,] and [MATH: s+t=7.] From this, we can find [MATH: t] as follows:
[MATH: t = (t+s) - s =7 - 5 = 2]

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get
[MATH: P(X ≤ 7|X > 5)|= 1 − e^{− λt}; = 1 − e^{− (4) ⋅ (2)}; = 1 − e^{− 8}; ≈ 0.999664.]
